en: The Sūtra on the Four Vows Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the lay devotee Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi country during the Wu dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī together with five hundred bhikṣus.
The Bhikṣu sat beneath a nyagrodha tree, preaching the Dharma for tens of millions of people.
At that time, there was a prominent elder in the city whose wealth was beyond measure; his name was Cunda.
Cunda had a son, fourteen years of age, who at that time fell gravely ill; unable to escape his affliction, he subsequently passed away.
His parents, brothers, and all his kinsmen, both near and distant, did not fail to hold him in deep affection and esteem; their weeping and grief were such as can hardly be described!
At that time, having heard that the Buddha had come to convert them, Cunda was filled with great joy and said to his wife:
"The Buddha is here now; we ought to go and see him."
"Those who hear the Buddha preach the Dharma will all be liberated and gladdened; they will forget their sorrows and eliminate their afflictions!
Thereupon, together with his wife, kinsmen, and servants, he went to where the Buddha was, paid homage to the Buddha, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The elder Cunda knelt with his hands joined in reverence and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:

"When people dwell in this world, they amass wealth through diligent toil and hardship, not daring to spend it on food or clothing, yet remaining ignorant of giving, upholding the sutras and precepts, and making no distinction between the honorable and the lowly."

Suppose one who has obtained their heart's desires should at some time reach the end of their life; when their parents, brothers, wife, children, and kinsmen weep and are consumed by grief, providing for their funeral rites and sending them off with wealth, treasures, clothing, and food—would these truly benefit the deceased?
The Buddha addressed Cunda and the disciples gathered in the assembly:
"Listen to what I shall say; contemplate it well!
Cunda’s kinsmen and all the disciples in the assembly each joined their palms and, with single-minded devotion, received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:
"Human beings have four wishes that cannot be permanently maintained.
What are these four?
"The first vow is this: regarding the human body, one always provides it first with bathing, adornment, food, and the five pleasures; yet when illness suddenly arrives, it cannot be prevented."
"When life ends, the body remains stiff upon the ground; it does not follow the soul as it departs. What benefit is there in vainly cherishing and valuing it?
"The second vow concerns the possession of wealth, official rank, and emoluments."
Those who obtain them rejoice; those who do not obtain them suffer grief and anxiety.

When illness strikes and death arrives as life comes to an end, all one's wealth, official rank, and emoluments remain behind in the world; they do not follow the soul of the deceased, serving only as a source of empty sorrow and suffering.
"The third vow refers to having parents, brothers, wives, children, paternal and maternal relatives, friends, acquaintances, affectionate ties, and prosperity and joy."
When illness strikes and my life comes to its end, they will be unable to save my life, nor can they follow my soul and spirit as it departs.
They will merely weep in vain, escort me to a deep grave outside the city, abandon me there, and each quickly return home.

Although they may remember me with sorrow, suffering, and anxious thought for no more than ten days, the various family clans and their sons and daughters will gather together, dancing and singing toward one another, joyfully partaking of food and drink, laughing and conversing face-to-face, casting the dead person entirely from their minds.

Although one has parents, brothers, wife, children, relatives near and far, friends, and acquaintances, they cannot accompany me when my life ends; their empty lamentations—what benefit would they bring?
"The fourth vow concerns the human mind.

Among the people of the world, few are able to guard their minds; they all let their minds run wild and indulge themselves, becoming lustful for the five pleasures, greedy for profit, quick to envy, prone to anger and strife, and lacking faith in the Way and its Virtue."

When one’s life ends and the body dies, the soul departs; these three follow one another in pursuit, unable to be separated from each other. It is like a sparrow flying, with its mind following its two wings: the mind is the spirit of the body, and the two wings are the *hun* and *po* souls.

If people cannot guard their minds, they act entirely from evil thoughts—committing killing, stealing, greed, and sexual misconduct—and due to the sins committed during their lives, they enter the Mount Tai hell after death and become hungry ghosts.
When their offenses have been exhausted, they emerge as animals, destined to be slaughtered and dismembered by humans.
Because they acted with a dissolute mind and indulged in their own desires, they enter the three evil realms.
The Buddha addressed Cunda and his disciples:
"Rectify your mind and guard your thoughts!
Reflect deeply within yourself:
know that this body is not your own, and that all material wealth likewise does not belong to you."

One should carefully examine all that one possesses—parents, brothers, wives, children, the five kinds of relatives, friends, acquaintances, official rank, and emoluments—and reflect that one desires to obtain them without ever feeling satisfied, thinking they are beneficial to one's person. Yet when old age, sickness, and death arrive, none of these can benefit one's person, nor can they avert them.
A person cannot extricate themselves from worldly entanglements to practice the Way, just as a parrot bird, out of attachment to its plumage and tail, falls into the hands of hunters.
The wise understand clearly that these four wishes do not accompany the human soul after death; to strive for them in vain is but a source of suffering.
By uprooting the source of affection and craving, one cuts off the paths to the three evil realms and attains the three good realms:
first, no further aging; second, no further illness; [and third, no further death].
"Third, one shall no longer die.
By firmly guarding one's mind, one may attain deliverance!
Upon hearing this sutra, the disciples were filled with joy and prostrated themselves before the Buddha.

In the *Sūtra on the Four Vows Spoken by the Buddha*, the Buddha contemplates the heavens, the earth, and the eight directions beyond: all things that receive their nature harbor sorrow and suffering; they constantly afflict the people and all sentient beings who crawl and move, for none can attain self-mastery.
Those who contend with Heaven for their allotted lifespan must all return to death.
Their bones and flesh will decay and rot, sinking beneath the earth;
their spirit will fly forth, wandering through the five realms of existence—ascending to heaven for doing good, and entering the abyss for committing evil.
In the life of any person, whatever good or evil they have committed, their spirit, essence, soul, and breath follow accordingly according to their calamities or blessings.
If during life one was filial and obedient toward one's parents and loyal and trustworthy in serving one's ruler, upon death one shall ascend to heaven.
Just as people in the world accumulate merit and perform good deeds, or serve in government seeking official rank until they reach the status of dukes, marquises, or the wealthy and noble—
whether one experiences wealth and joy or poverty, meanness, and distress— all of this is due to past karma.
To practice slaughter and cruel oppression is to be an evil person in life and receive heavy retribution in death.
Acting as one's own lord, the heart invites a hundred calamities; the joy of satisfying its desires will inevitably lead to future suffering.
Both sovereigns and the people are equally deluded regarding the Way.
Entrusting themselves to their parents,
they find that practicing good brings blessings and longevity, while committing evil leads to poverty and suffering.

Those who steal and deceive others, fail to repay their debts, or do not return borrowed goods shall, after death, become slaves, oxen, or horses; or they may become large pigs, whose bodies will be slaughtered, butchered, and flayed, weighed and sold to repay their creditors.

If one acts with stinginess and greed and refuses to practice giving, they will become a hungry ghost after death; unable to obtain food or clothing, they will be like a beggar who cuts off their own flesh with a knife and bows their head in supplication for sustenance.
All of these were, in their previous lives, greedy, cruel, rebellious, and did not believe in doing good. They committed injury, killing, theft, and adultery;

they slandered others with double-tongued speech, drank wine, and incited strife. Upon death, they entered hell, where they were beaten with whips, burned, and boiled; their bodies were further afflicted by the venom of stinging insects, and their suffering was boundless.

Human beings have six anxieties, three sufferings, and four pains; the Buddha gathered them in and transformed them so that the cycle of birth and death would cease. He abandoned his kingdom and renounced his kingship to seek the Way of spontaneity, accumulating merit for many years until he finally attained the truth of the Way.

The divine spirit shines through with clarity, seeing everything beyond the vast voids of heaven and earth; it knows the speech of humans, birds, beasts, insects, and creeping creatures, as well as the inclinations of their hearts.
The Buddha reflects that when a person dies, it is like a great wind suddenly arriving without any fixed time.
When death arrives at an unforeseen time, one must contend with the mind; perform good deeds without hesitation.
The Buddha uses the Way of the Sūtras to exhort the worthy: what benefit do rare and precious jewels bring to oneself if they are neither seen by the eyes nor heard by the ears?

All who pursue the Way should believe in the scriptures and precepts, guarding their goodness until death and refraining from committing evil in life; the Way must not be lost, and virtue must not be forsaken.
To distance oneself from the Way and lose one's virtue is like a child born without a mother, or a fish cast out from the deep.

When a person dies and is reborn, it is like a silkworm within a chaotic cocoon; having pierced the silk, it emerges and flies away. Its spirit remains the same, though it transforms its form and sheds its shell.
The Way is perfected through the subtle; by observing the five precepts, one gains the root.
The disciple, having heard the sutra, rejoiced and received the instruction with reverence; this constitutes knowing feelings (vedanā) as they truly are through essential awareness.
What is the awareness of perception (saṃjñā)?
It consists of the six perceptions of the body.
The eye conditions thought; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind condition thought.
These are the six types of thought.
What is the condition for the arising of thought?
The cessation of volitional formations is the cessation of perception; such is the knowledge of the cessation of perception.
What is the knowledge of the cessation of perception?
The cessation of volitional formations is the knowledge of the cessation of perception; such is the knowledge of the cessation of perception.
What is the consciousness that exhausts the perception of ideation?
This is the consciousness of the eightfold practice.

Consciousness cognizes; when one sees the truth and attains concentration of mind through the truths, these constitute the eight. In this way, the perception of ideation is exhausted through the practice of consciousness.
What is the cognition of the gratification of volitional formations?
That which arises from the causal condition of volitional formations as pleasure and rapture—this is the cognition of the gratification of volitional formations.
What is the cognition of the danger of volitional formations?
Regarding the thought that is impermanent, subject to exhaustion, suffering, and subject to change—this is called the consciousness of the thought.
What is the essential consciousness of the thought?

That which contemplates desire and greed as something to be understood, desire and greed as something to be severed, and desire and greed as something from which one can cross over by oneself—this is called the essential consciousness of the thought.
What is the consciousness of birth and death?

It is the consciousness of birth and death of the six bases: the consciousness of birth and death of the eye, and the formations of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; such is the consciousness of birth and death.
What is the knowledge of the origin of birth-and-death, the origin of cessation, and the origin of birth-and-death?
What is the knowledge of the exhaustion of birth-and-death?
The exhaustion of cessation is the knowledge of the exhaustion of birth-and-death.
What is the consciousness of practice for the exhaustion of desire regarding birth and death?

It is the consciousness of the eightfold path; seeing the truths and attaining the concentration on the truths constitutes these eight. Such is the consciousness of practice for the cessation of desire regarding birth and death.
What is the consciousness of the flavor of birth and death?
That which gives rise to feelings of pleasure and joy through the causal conditions of birth and death—this is the consciousness of the flavor of birth and death.
What is the consciousness of the core of birth and death?
All that is subject to birth and death, impermanent, ending in suffering, and subject to change—this is the "brain-consciousness" (mūla-vijñāna) of birth and death.
What is the "essential consciousness" (sāra-vijñāna) of birth and death?
That which is the craving for birth and death, following after such craving, and that which is capable of severing it and crossing over it—this is the essential consciousness of birth and death.
What are the six bases of consciousness within the aggregate of consciousness?
They are eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness; these are known as the consciousnesses of consciousness.
What is the origination of consciousness?
The origination of the life-force and name is the origination of consciousness; such is the origination of consciousness.
What is the cessation of consciousness as consciousness?
The designation "exhaustion" refers to the exhaustion of consciousness; such is the exhaustion of consciousness.
What is the practice for the complete exhaustion of consciousness?

There are eight practices: from right view up to right concentration as the eighth—such is the practice for the complete exhaustion of desire and consciousness, which is the consciousness that accords with reality.

What is the tasting of consciousness? It is the arising of pleasure and joy in the mind due to the object of consciousness; such is the tasting of its arising, which constitutes the knowing of the tasting of consciousness.
What is the head of consciousness? It is that by which the object of consciousness is known.
To exhaust, to suffer, and to turn away—thus is the consciousness that knows the brain.
What is the essential consciousness that knows what is to be known?
That which can sustain sensual desire and can sever and transcend sensual desire—thus is the essential consciousness.
"In this way, bhikṣus, there are seven points for full comprehension. What are the seven?
Form, its arising, its cessation, the path, its gratification, its suffering, and its escape—
these are the seven aspects for each of the five aggregates.
What are the three contemplations regarding consciousness?
There are also seven matters by which one acquires the five aggregates (skandhas) and forms the six bases of decay (āyatana).
Contemplating the body as form is the first; contemplating the five aggregates is the second; contemplating the six bases of decay is the third; therefore, they are called the three contemplations.

A bhikṣu who is able to understand these seven points and is also capable of the three contemplations will, before long, practice until he falls upon the path and severs the fetters. Being without fetters, his mind is liberated and he lives with wisdom; seeing the path and seeing the essential, he attains realization and abides in cessation. Having already severed birth and death, his mental activities and volitions shall no longer return to saṃsāra; he has attained the Way.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
The bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
